draft.title: Courts and NGOs in protecting the environment
card: Courts hear environmental disputes and apply the law. The NSW Land and Environment Court is a specialist court that hears cases about planning, development and environmental offences.
Courts can decide whether a decision or activity followed the law. Depending on the case, they can order a person or business to stop, to fix damage, or to pay a penalty.
A non-government organisation (NGO) is a group that is independent of government. Environmental NGOs include groups such as Greenpeace and the Australian Conservation Foundation.
NGOs campaign to change public opinion and laws. They can take legal action in court, and they monitor compliance by watching whether governments and businesses keep to the law and to their promises.
draft.remember: Courts apply and enforce environmental law. NGOs push for it, test it in court and check it is followed.

a.q: An environmental NGO watches a mine's reports to check that the mine is keeping to its approval conditions. Which role is the NGO performing?
opts: Monitoring compliance
Hearing the case
Passing the law
Setting the penalty
a.why: Watching whether a business follows the law and its conditions is monitoring compliance. Hearing cases and setting penalties are done by courts, not by NGOs.
a.clue: The NGO is checking, not deciding.

b.q: Residents in Newcastle believe a council approved a development without following the planning law. A local environmental NGO files a case in the Land and Environment Court. Which statement best describes what is happening?
opts: The NGO takes legal action and the court decides the case
The NGO decides the case and the court campaigns
The court takes legal action and the NGO decides the case
The NGO and the court both make the law in this case
b.why: The NGO uses the court by starting legal action, and the court hears the dispute and decides whether the law was followed. The roles are not reversed: NGOs do not decide cases, and the court does not campaign.
b.clue: Who brings the case, and who judges it?

b.best: The NGO takes legal action and the court decides the case

problems.detail: The stem says the NGO is there 'to check that the mine is keeping to its approval conditions', which nearly repeats the card's definition of monitoring compliance. The clue 'checking, not deciding' then points straight at the answer. With distractors that are plainly not NGO roles, students can answer by matching words rather than understanding the role. That is easy for Year 12 HSC.

proposal.title: Courts and NGOs in protecting the environment
card: Courts hear environmental disputes and apply the law. The NSW Land and Environment Court is a specialist court that hears cases about planning, development and environmental offences.
Courts can decide whether a decision or activity followed the law. They can enforce it: depending on the case, they can order a person or business to stop, to fix damage, or to pay a penalty.
A non-government organisation (NGO) is a group that is independent of government. Environmental NGOs include groups such as Greenpeace and the Australian Conservation Foundation.
NGOs campaign to change public opinion and laws. They can take legal action in court, and they monitor compliance by watching whether governments and businesses keep to the law and to their promises.
proposal.remember: Courts apply and enforce environmental law. NGOs push for it, test it in court and check it is followed.

a.q: Each month, an environmental NGO reads a coal mine's water test results and compares them with the limits set in the mine's approval. What is the NGO mainly doing?
opts: Monitoring compliance with the approval
Taking legal action against the mine
Campaigning to change the law
Enforcing the approval conditions
a.why: Comparing results with the approval limits is watching whether the mine keeps to the law, which is monitoring compliance. Enforcing is tempting, but an NGO cannot order the mine to stop or pay a penalty: that power belongs to courts. No case has been filed and no campaign has begun.
a.clue: Has the NGO gone to court or to the public yet?

b.q: Residents in Newcastle believe a council approved a development without following the planning law. A local environmental NGO files a case in the Land and Environment Court. Which statement best describes what is happening?
opts: The NGO takes legal action and the court decides the case
The NGO decides the case and the court campaigns
The court takes legal action and the NGO decides the case
The NGO and the court both make the law in this case
b.why: The NGO uses the court by starting legal action, and the court hears the dispute and decides whether the law was followed. The roles are not reversed: NGOs do not decide cases, and the court does not campaign.
b.clue: Who brings the case, and who judges it?

why: the fresh check found a problem

b.best: The NGO takes legal action and the court decides the case

problems.detail: The why says the power to order a mine to stop or pay a penalty 'belongs to courts'. In NSW, regulators such as the EPA can also issue prevention notices, stop-work orders and penalty notices. Better: 'an NGO has no power to order the mine to stop or pay a penalty'.

Each wrong option swaps the roles in an obviously absurd way, such as a court campaigning or an NGO deciding a case. A Year 12 student can reject them without understanding the idea, so the question is too easy for HSC level.

check.summary: The card and answers are sound. Why (a) wrongly suggests only courts can order stops or penalties, when regulators like the EPA can too, and question b's wrong options are too obviously absurd for Year 12.

Question b, level: Each wrong option swaps the roles in an obviously absurd way, such as a court campaigning or an NGO deciding a case. A Year 12 student can reject them without understanding the idea, so the question is too easy for HSC level.
